components.note: GS Defs 1.1-1.3 (pp. 18-25): outcomes, events, distribution function m with P(E)=sum over E, uniform distribution. The handbook supplies the mass function, induced measure, conventions, support/null/almost-sure notions, and identifies both declared variants: GS's term 'distribution function' (lines 51-53, verified Def. 1.2 p. 19) and the function-based random variable (lines 16-17). Boundary: outcomes of mass zero may remain (line 47), worked in lines 166-168.

GS Thms 1.1, 1.2, 1.4 and Cor. 1.1 (pp. 22-24) are all present (Cor. 1.1 as the decomposition in annex line 32); the m=0 case and the null/support criterion are worked; the converse atomic representation has written steps.

GS Def. 4.3 (p. 142) joint random variable and joint distribution, Ex. 4.11 (impossible tuples get probability 0, matched by lines 94-95), marginal distributions (Ex. 4.13). The pair definition is stated explicitly; the n-tuple joint variable of Def. 4.3 is the law of the finite-valued tuple map, which the general definition (lines 78-86) and the grouping theorem cover.
GS grouping of outcomes by a common value (Ex. 6.6, p. 229) and marginal distributions (Ex. 4.13): event, marginal and image-law formulas with written proofs including empty fibers.

GS conditional distribution m(w|E)=m(w)/P(E) on E, zero off E, requiring P(E)>0, and P(F|E)=P(F and E)/P(E) (p. 134); the relative-magnitude justification and GS's caveat that a conditioned model is only useful if all relevant information is used (Ex. 4.3) are matched by lines 132-135.
GS multiplication rule (4.2) and conditional distribution as a distribution; chain rule and successive conditioning with written proofs and the null-final-intersection boundary (annex lines 103-106).
Worked boundary for GS's requirement P(E)>0 (p. 134): 0/0 ratio, failure of the multiplication equation to determine a value, almost-sure event omitting outcomes.

components.gap: GS's odds presentation (sec. 1.2 'Odds', pp. 27-28, Def. 1.4 and Ex. 1.12) treats the odds in favour of E as a pair r:s of which only the ratio matters, gives both directions (r/s = p/(1-p) and, conversely, p = r/(r+s)), and reads them from acceptable bets (a bet at r to 1 odds means P(E) = r/(r+1)). Lines 183-184 give only the one-way ratio P(G)/(1-P(G)); the odds-to-probability inverse, the r:s form and the betting reading are not supplied. Secondary: GS's hypotheses (p. 145) are any pairwise disjoint events with union Omega, while line 173 requires each hypothesis to be nonempty without identifying this narrowing.

components.note: GS total probability (4.3), Thm 1.3 and Bayes' formula (pp. 145-146) with zero-prior hypotheses handled and the odds form proved; q1=0 and the requirement q0>0 are worked.

components.gap: GS sec. 4.1 (pp. 139-143): Def. 4.2 gives mutual independence of A1,...,An together with an equivalent form over every choice of each event or its complement (P of the intersection of the chosen sets equals the product); the text states that the single identity P(A1 and ... and An) = P(A1)...P(An) does not imply mutual independence (Exercise 8) and that the outcomes of a Bernoulli trials process form mutually independent events; Def. 4.4 defines mutual independence of n random variables X1,...,Xn by P(X1=r1,...,Xn=rn) = product of P(Xi=ri). Lines 219-240 define independence for only two random variables, the complement form appears only for pairs (lines 246-247), and the full-product-identity and Bernoulli-trials claims are absent.

GS 'Independent Trials Processes' (p. 144, Def. 4.5; Exs 4.14-4.15, pp. 144-145): n mutually independent, identically distributed variables built on R x ... x R from the product distribution m(w) = m(w1)...m(wn), with Bernoulli trials and the binomial law P(Sn=j) = C(n,j) p^j q^(n-j) as instances. The product construction (lines 252-255; annex lines 188-198) builds only a two-factor product S x T, so the n-fold product model, the mutual independence of its n coordinates and the Bernoulli/binomial instance are not supplied. The Thm 4.1 criterion and complement pairs are otherwise covered.

components.note: GS Def. 6.1 (p. 226) expected value/mean; the value-sum form is proved in thm:p15-finite-expectation-laws; existence is automatic for finite spaces (line 460).
GS Thm 6.1 (p. 230), Thm 6.2 with the induction to finite sums and the remark that independence is not needed (pp. 231-232), Thm 6.4 (p. 233); all with written finite proofs.
Indicator counting E[N] = sum P(Ai) without independence (GS's method in Thm 6.3 and Ex. 6.8) and the non-factorization counterpart of GS Ex. 6.10.

GS Def. 6.2 (p. 239) E(X|F) = sum x_j P(X=x_j|F) is the expectation under the conditional mass function p_B, i.e. the grouping theorem applied to the finite space (Omega, P_B); E[X|Y] with an explicit null-fiber convention.
GS Thm 6.5 (pp. 239-240) with null blocks handled; averaging property and a.s. uniqueness proved; worked alert computation.

components.gap: The chapter claims to develop 'the finite part of the discrete treatment' of GS secs 1.2, 4.1, 6.1 (lines 12-15), but this scope statement (lines 453-467) neither develops nor places elsewhere several finite topics of those sections: independent trials processes, Bernoulli trials and the binomial law (4.1, pp. 144-145) with E(Sn) = np (6.1, Thm 6.3, p. 233); fair games/martingales defined by conditional expectation (6.1, Ex. 6.15, p. 241). It also omits GS's normative and empirical account of choosing a model's weights (1.2, pp. 26-28): there is no single correct sample space (two-coin example, the uniform law on {0,1,2} being 'not consistent with observed data on coin tossing'); symmetry often suggests uniform weights but ignorance alone does not justify them; weights may be fixed by statistical observation (newborn boys about .513, a figure that may change with new studies and vary between countries); and personal probabilities can be read from acceptable betting odds. Lines 454-458 state only that a justified model is required.
source_locators: GS sec. 6.1 Thm 6.3 p. 233, Martingales p. 241

components.gap: Durrett's Exercises 1.5.5 (p. 28) and 1.6.13 (p. 37) replace the nonnegativity hypothesis of monotone convergence by integrability of the first negative part: if g_n increases to g and the integral of g_1^- is finite then the integrals of g_n increase to that of g; if E X_1^- < infinity and X_n increases to X then E X_n increases to E X. This hypothesis variant is not stated in the theorem (lines 81-90) or anywhere on the input route; lines 260-262 show only that monotonicity alone does not suffice. Its only rendering is in uninserted w02c files.

components.gap: Durrett's Exercise 1.5.10 (p. 28) gives the signed series interchange: if the sum over n of the integrals of |f_n| is finite then sum_n of the integrals of f_n equals the integral of sum_n f_n. The theorem (lines 92-116) states the series formula only for nonnegative f_n (covering Exercises 1.4.1, 1.5.4, 1.5.6, 1.6.15, Lemma 1.4.5 and Fatou, Thm 1.5.5); the absolutely summable signed variant is not supplied on the input route.
source_locators: Durrett Lemma 1.4.5 p. 22, Thm 1.5.5 p. 26, Exercises 1.5.4, 1.5.6, 1.5.10 p. 28

components.gap: Durrett fixes notation for special cases of the integral (pp. 23-24): the integral of f(x)dx for Lebesgue measure on R^d; the integral from a to b of f(x)dx for the integral over [a,b] against Lebesgue measure; the integral of f(x)dG(x) for the measure with mass G(b)-G(a) on (a,b]; and sum_i f(i) for counting measure on a countable set, 'to indicate that results for sums follow from those for integrals'. Neither this definition nor the chapter introduces these notations or the counting-measure reading of sums, although later chapters write integrals as f(x,y)dx.
source_locators: Durrett Step 4 and 'Notation for special cases', pp. 22-24

components.gap: Durrett's definition of convergence in measure (p. 26) carries the claim that on a space of finite measure it is a weaker assumption than convergence a.e. (a.e. convergence implies convergence in measure when the total measure is finite). The definition (lines 197-217) neither states nor proves this; the input route has only the probability-space case, in a later chapter this entry does not reference (limit-theorems-and-concentration-w02b-p15-013.tex lines 194-202).

components.gap: Durrett Thm 1.6.8 (p. 31) and its p > 1 special case are covered with full proof.
